The root cause was a crimping die at Voltaris that was replaced in July and not re-qualified. The resulting undersized crimps raised contact resistance at the connector to 4–6 times nominal, which made the connector overheat [1].

The chain, from the 5 Whys in the report:
- Contact resistance at the crimp was 4 to 6 times nominal.
- Crimp height was below the connector maker's specification.
- A crimping die at Voltaris was replaced in July and not re-qualified.
- Voltaris pull tests were sampled once per shift instead of once per reel, so the fault was not caught there.
- Arvenne's incoming inspection checked voltage and capacity, not crimps, so it was not caught there either [1].

All affected bikes were built with Voltaris lot VL-2507-B [1][2]. Pup bikes use Kelda Energy packs and are not affected [1].</answer>

Front-loader net revenue (Barge and Barge 2 combined, Delivered lines only, in euros) fell from about €4.29M in Q3 to about €1.64M in Q4 2025, a drop of about €2.65M (about 62%) [1][2]. Units fell from 1,217 to 437 [1][2].

- Q3 (1 Jul–30 Sep): €4,293,994.51 from 752 lines [1].
- Q4 (1 Oct–31 Dec): €1,641,068.23 from 265 lines [2].

CHF and GBP amounts are converted at the budget rates (0.94 CHF and 0.85 GBP per EUR), with discounts applied per line [3][4].

The documents do not state the cause. Context: the first-generation Barge stopped being sold on 30 September [5][6], and Barge 2 became available only from 1 October [7]. Q3 also included the August summer closure [8][9]. These facts fit a model changeover, but no source says it caused the drop.

Pédalo Logistique took delivery of the most bikes among fleet customers in 2025: 45 bikes across 2 delivered order lines [1]. Counting only Delivered lines, as the sales README requires for unit figures [2], the next are Stadtbote Berlin (35) and GreenDrop London (32) [1]. GreenDrop London placed the most bikes in total (48), but 16 of them were not delivered (Cancelled or Returned) [3].

About €122,044 of fleet discounts on delivered 2025 orders: €103,058 on 14 EUR lines plus £16,138 on 3 GBP lines, which is €18,986 at 0.85 GBP per EUR [1][2]. This is calculated as quantity × unit price × discount %, the discount value as the sales README defines it. Cancelled and returned lines are excluded [1]. The figure comes from the orders file as stored; the December board minutes say final revenue will come from the January order export [3], and I found no later confirmation that the file is final.</answer>

About €79,573 in extra net revenue (EUR, estimated) on delivered Mule orders placed from 1 July 2025. Actual net revenue on those 513 lines (712 bikes) was about €2,089,649, against about €2,010,076 at the pre-increase prices [1]. The pre-increase prices of €3,575 (EUR), CHF 3,590 and GBP 3,050 are shown on June 2025 Mule orders [2][3][4]. The board set the rise at 4% from 1 July, rounded to the nearest 10 in local currency [5], and the budget uses 4% [6]. Local amounts were converted at the budget rates (÷0.94 CHF, ÷0.85 GBP) [7][6]. The figure is a like-for-like price effect: it assumes the same volume at the old price and does not account for any change in demand, which the sources do not cover.

No, the field test does not support the 120 km claim. The tester's summary on page 3 says "range at 200 kg in heat way below the 120 km claim" [1]. That test ran in 31°C heat with a 200 kg load on a long climb, where the motor derated after 28 minutes and the battery fell from 100% to 4% [1].
